A repeated hexadecimal digit d represents the byte 16d + d = 17d, so every shorthand-expressible channel is one of the 16 multiples of 17. The similarity objective is the negative sum of three independent squared channel errors, making its global maximum exactly the combination of the nearest valid value for each channel. For byte value v, (v + 8) // 17 rounds to the nearest multiple's digit: adjacent levels are 17 apart, their midpoint is a half-integer, and an integer byte therefore has no tie. Values from 0 through 255 map within digit indices 0 through 15. Parsing each channel, formatting the selected digit in lowercase, repeating it twice, and retaining the leading hash produces the unique optimal six-digit color.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 800, Python, and the native similarRGB(color) interface. Authenticated source evidence confirms a seven-character #RRGGBB input, a leading hash, lowercase hexadecimal digits after it, #XYZ shorthand expanding to #XXYYZZ, similarity as the negative sum of three squared channel differences, and a six-digit shorthand-expressible return. The statement accepts any co-optimal answer; because adjacent repeated-digit bytes differ by 17, an integer channel cannot tie, so the protected solution still returns the unique optimum.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2066208742 are algorithmically identical: both inspect channel starts 1, 3, and 5, parse the same hexadecimal bytes, compute the same (value + 8) // 17 digit, format it in lowercase, repeat it, prepend a hash, and join the result. The authenticated contract fixes every legal input at exactly three two-digit channels, so it provides no source workload dimension for an honest runtime trend. solution_quality_findings: The protected app source introduces the exact generic local name index for a row and character position in source while constructing the next-occurrence table. solution_quality_findings: The protected one-line implementation is the canonical shifted-binary solution and is expert-interview ready. It exposes the mathematical identity directly, has no unnecessary state or control flow, uses the contract name num, and preserves the app-local solve(num) interface. A candidate would add ceremony without materially improving clarity, correctness, or complexity, so none was created.

Positive binary integers partition into groups with one leading bit followed by every fixed-width suffix. Replacing num by q = num + 1 selects the corresponding positive binary integer; deleting its leading one therefore returns precisely the offset within the correct length group. For num = 0, q is one and deleting that sole data bit correctly returns the empty string.

An independent repeated-division oracle, an independently derived length-group/offset construction, a separate per-bit construction control, the protected app source, and the immutable native source agreed on all ten visible cases, every num from 0 through 1,000,000, and 50,060 deterministic random and boundary values. The latter set included both legal endpoints and every shifted power-of-two group start and group end through the maximum output width.

The former three-tier benchmark was defective: a correct O((log q)^2) bit-position control passed its output checks and scaling verdict, while the documented O(q log q) enumeration alternative cannot reasonably finish the required visible num = 10^9 boundary. Because legal outputs contain at most 29 bits, timing cannot provide an honest trend. The benchmark was replaced by a strictly validated asymptotic-optimality certificate: every result has floor(log2(q)) characters for q > 1, giving an output lower bound of Omega(log q), and the protected single conversion plus slice gives the matching O(log q) upper bound.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution counts distinct nonempty substrings using a Suffix Automaton (SAM). Building a Suffix Automaton for a string of length n creates at most 2n - 1 states with amortized O(n) transition updates for a fixed 26-character alphabet, giving O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts string s and returns the total integer count of distinct nonempty contiguous substrings.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution finds the lexicographically largest length-k contiguous subarray from an array nums of unique integers. solution_quality_findings: The protected SQL solution inner joins Candidates and Rounds on interview_id, filters WHERE years_of_exp >= 2, groups by candidate_id, and filters HAVING SUM(score) > 15 ORDER BY candidate_id. The single-pass join and aggregate query is canonical, concise, and optimal; no candidate is required.

WHERE years_of_exp >= 2 pre-filters candidates to those meeting the experience threshold. Inner joining Rounds connects each candidate to all their interview round scores. GROUP BY candidate_id HAVING SUM(score) > 15 accurately computes total interview score and retains only candidates with totals strictly exceeding 15.

Joining C candidates and R round rows takes expected O(C + R) time, and grouping and sorting qualifying candidates takes O(C log C) time. Working space is O(C + R). Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Outputs single column candidate_id, requires years_of_exp >= 2, checks strict score sum > 15, and includes candidate_id ordering.

The approach accurately details pre-filtering candidates by experience, joining rounds, grouping by candidate_id, and applying HAVING SUM(score) > 15. Alternatives and edge cases cover pre-aggregating rounds, correlated score subqueries, exactly 2 years qualifying, total score 15 vs 16, candidates without round rows, multi-round summation, and shared interview IDs.
App SQL and native SQL solutions are identical with SHA-256 digest dab2aa3f29b6fb12d4769dfc60221dd18c7fe77cca2e21c40442f4b10a6d3be3. Verified submission remains untouched.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution traverses the linked list starting at head. When current.next is negative, it detaches current.next and prepends it to head (updating head), while keeping current on non-negative nodes. This sorts the linked list in linear time O(N) and O(1) auxiliary space without comparison sorting; no candidate is required.

Since nodes are given sorted by absolute value, non-negative nodes are already in non-decreasing order, while negative nodes encountered later have larger magnitudes (more negative values). Prepending each negative node to head reverses the negative nodes into correct non-decreasing signed order ahead of the non-negative chain.
Each node is inspected and relinked at most once in a single pass, using O(N) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts a ListNode head sorted by absolute value, relinks existing nodes in-place, and returns the head of the sorted list.

The approach accurately details relative sign ordering, prepending negative nodes to head, and O(N) time / O(1) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover collecting/sorting values, insertion sort, non-negative lists, all-negative lists, equal absolute value ties, zero placement, duplicate values, and single-node lists.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the exact same single-pass negative node prepending algorithm with SHA-256 digests 45fc7d0c04a8e93ecc14847b02396f41f18cf93d6cb4d220164b06115eec0c10 and 096e7a173fae82bf7e1fbb06c40c2467a05e3aeb695d3214d65c3c2f63e308be. Verified submission remains untouched.

WHERE amount > 500 filters for bills strictly exceeding 500. COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) ensures that each customer with at least one qualifying bill is counted exactly once.

Scanning B bill rows and performing distinct customer aggregation takes O(B log B) or expected O(B) time and O(C) working space for C qualifying distinct customers. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Outputs single column rich_count, excludes amount = 500, and deduplicates multiple qualifying bills for the same customer.

The approach accurately details filtering by strict threshold amount > 500, deduplicating via COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id), and relational complexity bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover group-then-count subqueries, non-distinct row counting errors, conditional distinct aggregation, amount = 500 boundary values, mixed bills for a customer, and empty/zero results.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution uses a hash dictionary self.videos for active video records, a min-heap self.available_ids for recycled deleted IDs, and a counter self.next_id for new IDs. Operations upload, remove, watch, like, dislike, getLikesAndDislikes, and getViews execute in optimal O(log Q + C) time and O(U + Q) space; no candidate is required.

Upload pops from available_ids min-heap when non-empty, otherwise uses next_id, guaranteeing smallest available ID reuse. Remove deletes from self.videos (if present) and pushes the ID to available_ids. Watch clamps endMinute to string length and increments view count. Statistic methods handle missing IDs with sentinels [-1], -1, and '-1'.

Heap upload/remove operations take O(log Q) time. Watch takes O(C) for returning C characters. Overall time complexity across Q operations is O(Q log Q + C) with O(U + Q) space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Implements all VideoSharingPlatform methods with accurate ID assignment, view clamping, statistics tracking, and missing-video sentinels.

The approach accurately details separating active content from reusable IDs, heap ID management, and O(Q log Q + C) time / O(U + Q) space complexity. Alternatives and edge cases cover scanning for gaps, search trees, monotone counters, repeated removals, ID reuse resetting statistics, watch range clamping, missing ID sentinels, and counter independence.

App Python and native Python solutions use the same min-heap and hash dictionary design with SHA-256 digests bbf4ec2e72632d07da1329110d216a7a5f24d16f0f4f402954eeb83417622765 and 8e8df77f924674ae27e4da1b00cedbdff37fc52dfe20f225749235e3f9304d10. Verified submission remains untouched.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution counts character frequencies with Counter(s), sorts the frequencies descending, and multiplies position i's frequency by (i // 9 + 1). Assigning highest frequencies to cheap key positions (1st 9 get cost 1, 2nd 9 get cost 2, last 8 get cost 3) is optimal and concise; no candidate is required.
By the exchange argument, pairing descending character frequencies with ascending slot press costs (1 for first 9 letters, 2 for next 9, 3 for last 8) minimizes total keypresses.

Counting s of length n takes O(n) time. Sorting 26 frequencies takes O(26 log 26) = O(1) time. Total time complexity is O(n) with O(1) auxiliary space for 26 alphabet counters. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts a lowercase string s and returns the minimum total keypresses across all valid 26-letter assignments to 9 buttons.

The approach accurately details multiset slot costs, greedy descending frequency pairing proof, and O(n) time / O(1) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover testing layouts, recounting per position, alphabetical assignment, 1..9 used letters, 10..18 used letters, 26 used letters, tied frequencies, absent letters, and single-letter strings.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the exact same greedy frequency counting algorithm with SHA-256 digests 4344f118126439645882001bf52621227f7fc67b7e1c2fe4d74223cff5ff360a and a15811d89929b94445dd1c70faed341539be61001edcfdf1ecc6efa52f6c49f2. Verified submission remains untouched.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution uses binary lifting LCA to find the tree median of start, end, and node for each query. Specifically, it computes lca(start, end), lca(start, node), and lca(end, node), returning the deepest node among the three. This resolves each query in O(log n) time after O(n log n) preprocessing; no candidate is required.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution sorts all grid cells (val, row, col) by value, and iterates through them maintaining row_max and col_max arrays. For each cell, score = max(row_max[r], col_max[c]) + 1, which is assigned to answer[r][c] and updates row_max[r] and col_max[c]. The greedy sorting solution runs in O(N log N) time and O(N) space; no candidate is required.

Since original grid values are distinct, sorting guarantees that all smaller elements in a cell's row and column are processed first. Assigning max(row_max[r], col_max[c]) + 1 gives each cell the minimal possible value that preserves row/column relative order.

Sorting N = m * n cell triples takes O(N log N) time. Updating row and column maxima takes O(N) time. Total time complexity is O(N log N) with O(N) auxiliary space for sorted cells and output matrix. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts m x n matrix grid, preserves row and column relative order, and returns a new m x n matrix minimizing the overall maximum value.

The approach accurately details sorting cell dependencies, tracking row_max and col_max arrays, greedy minimum score assignment, and O(N log N) time / O(N) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover DAG topological sorting, repeated minimum search, single row/column matrices, unrelated cells, single cell matrices, and distinct original values.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical greedy cell-sorting algorithm with SHA-256 digests 07e0e9e2d15e81678c7305e10a80274dc27cd318630fc3af64a3d6ae482aff74 and e50d999163070c574ae52e2021d9ee836ccfc47fa1e662981e63b68ce0120734. Verified submission remains untouched.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution uses two pointers (left and right) with running prefix and suffix sums (left_sum, right_sum). If left_sum == right_sum, both pointers move inward; if left_sum < right_sum, left moves right and accumulates nums[left], incrementing operation count; otherwise right moves left. The greedy two-pointer strategy runs in O(n) time and O(1) space; no candidate is required.

Since all elements are positive integers, accumulating into the smaller sum is strictly necessary to equalize left and right outer sums. Absorbing adjacent elements corresponds directly to 1 merge operation per step until pointers meet.
Both pointers move inward until left >= right, taking at most n steps in O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts nums list of positive integers, handles already-palindromic lists (returning 0) and single elements, and returns minimum required merge operations.

The approach accurately details mirrored contiguous group sums, smaller-side sum absorption greedy proof, and O(n) time / O(1) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover physical list mutation overhead, interval DP, already-palindromic arrays, single elements, unbalanced absorption, positivity requirement, and pointer crossing.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical greedy two-pointer prefix/suffix sum algorithm with SHA-256 digests f679b519a4652461005255dd2ff4b950294f410aa13eb360ef03ba3e1253a1cb and 6d967ab9bccc1f8501eef5a5992d7515b3660a2682be0f944d7d8289ab8c3ed1. solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution evaluates move costs for both valid target layouts: [0, 1, ..., n-1] (zero at start) and [1, 2, ..., n-1, 0] (zero at end). For each layout, it decomposes the permutation mapping into disjoint cycles: cycles of length L containing the zero element cost L - 1 moves, while cycles of length L > 1 without zero cost L + 1 moves. The solution runs in O(n) time and O(n) space; no candidate is required.

A permutation mapping index i -> target_pos(nums[i]) decomposes into disjoint cycles. The zero element acts as the single swap slot: a cycle containing zero rotates in L - 1 moves, while an external cycle requires 1 move to enter zero into the cycle and 1 move to exit, costing L + 1 moves total. Taking min over both target layouts strictly minimizes moves.
Tracing cycles for each target layout visits each position once, taking O(n) time total and O(n) auxiliary space for the seen array. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts nums permutation array, handles n=2 edge cases, and returns minimum moves to reach either sorted layout.

The approach accurately details cycle decomposition, empty-space cycle cost (L - 1), external cycle cost (L + 1), dual target layout evaluation, and O(n) time / O(n) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover legal swap simulations, quadratic unindexed searches, single-target fallacies, already-sorted arrays, fixed points, external cycles, and n=2 bounds.

App Python and native Python solutions both execute the identical permutation cycle decomposition algorithm for both zero-at-start and zero-at-end layouts with SHA-256 digests c7924149acc9855953b9afbba4ce2f880ec50851916b784fb071866f28d2c1ba and f8ce3eedaac88a1c2d0e3bd6b9553f7646dcce79ed602c1aaf02d2c2d9044f14. solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution uses dynamic programming with a rolling array of sets tracking reachable counts of ones for each grid cell. It first checks if the total path length (r + c - 1) is even, setting target = (r + c - 1) // 2. For each cell (r, c), it merges sets of reachable ones from (r-1, c) and (r, c-1) and adds grid[r][c], filtering out counts > target. The DP solution runs in O(r * c * (r + c)) time and O(c * (r + c)) space; no candidate is required.

Every valid path from (0,0) to (r-1, c-1) has length r + c - 1. An odd path length cannot be divided into equal numbers of 0s and 1s, returning False immediately. DP set propagation correctly calculates all reachable ones counts up to target.

At each of the r * c cells, sets of size at most O(r + c) are merged, yielding O(r * c * (r + c)) worst-case time complexity. Rolling array space uses O(c * (r + c)) space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts r x c binary matrix grid, returns boolean True if a balanced path exists and False otherwise.

The approach accurately details odd path length rejection, reachable ones count set propagation, rolling column array optimization, and O(r c (r+c)) time / O(c (r+c)) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover unmemoized DFS exponential explosion, 3D boolean tables, ones-minus-zeros tracking, odd path lengths, endpoint inclusion, and count deduplication.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution uses a Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) to count strictly smaller values on both sides of each index. In the first pass (left-to-right), it records smaller_left[i] = query(nums[i] - 1) and adds nums[i] to the tree. In the second pass (right-to-left), it checks query(nums[i] - 1) >= k and smaller_left[i] >= k. The solution runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space; no candidate is required.
Querying at nums[i] - 1 counts values strictly smaller than nums[i]. Performing two independent Fenwick passes correctly calculates left-side and right-side smaller element counts for every index.

Each of the n elements requires O(log n) Fenwick query and update operations in both passes, giving O(n log n) total time and O(n) auxiliary space for the tree and smaller_left array. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts nums array and integer k, returning total count of k-big indices.

The approach accurately details order statistic queries, Fenwick tree coordinate mapping (1 to n), dual pass structure, and O(n log n) time / O(n) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover direct side scans, merge-sort counting, strict inequality query adjustments, side boundary limits, and monotone arrays.

solution_quality_findings: The protected Python solution uses two deques (one for enter state 0, one for exit state 1) and simulates second-by-second door crossing while skipping empty time gaps. It maintains previous_direction (defaulting to 1/exit when idle). The event-driven queue simulation runs in O(n) time and O(n) space; no candidate is required.

When both queues have waiting people, the direction used in the previous second is prioritized. If that queue is empty, the other direction crosses. Idle gaps fast-forward current time to arrival[next_person] and reset previous_direction to 1 (exit). Non-decreasing arrival order ensures FIFO deques preserve index-order priority.

Each person is enqueued and dequeued exactly once, and empty gaps fast-forward directly, yielding O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space for the deques and answer array. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts arrival and state lists, returning an array of exact crossing times for each person in index order.

The approach accurately details two-queue FIFO state tracking, door priority logic (previous direction / default exit), time gap fast-forwarding, and O(n) time / O(n) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover unsorted list searches, second-by-second walking, idle second resets, same-second arrivals, same-direction index ties, empty preferred queues, and continuous backlogs.
